title: Introduction to International Relations and Diplomacy
description: This course aims to provide students with the analytical skills and critical knowledge to understand key concepts, principles and cases relating to international relations (IR) and diplomatic affairs. Students will be introduced to different kinds of literature, to make them familiar with the actors, goals, means, and consequences of state interaction in the field of international relations. This course will also explore a number of theoretical debates in diplomatic studies, and the practice of global diplomacy with a particular focus on its applicability in the contemporary world order.
outcome: After taking this course, students are expected to critically assess different theoretical approaches of international relations and diplomacy;  engage with debates in international affairs and diplomacy; apply various concepts in the practice of diplomacy;  engage with debates on political and diplomatic issues in international politics and present their distinctive viewpoints with evidence-based knowledge; and discuss diplomatic affairs in the international political context.
syllabus: Week 1: Introduction to international relations and diplomacyThis session will introduce a brief history of international relations and diplomacy in our global world. We will answer questions such as ‘Why do we have various different theories of international relations?’ and ‘What is diplomacy?’. Week 2: The rise of modern international order and global diplomacyThis session will examine the emergence of international orders and different theoretical approaches to international relations and apply various concepts to the practice of diplomacy. We will also discuss the relationship between great and small powers in international relations and global diplomacy. Week 3: Actors in international affairs and diplomacyThis session will focus on different actors in international relations and diplomacy. We will also discuss the complexity of contemporary international relations and the changing international environment that formulate foreign policies.  Week 4: International organizations in international affairs: The United NationsThis session will analyse the powers of the UN Security Council and General Assembly to authorize the use of force and  non-military sanctions in international relations. Week 5: Bilateral and Multilateral DiplomacyThis session will discuss how bilateral and multilateral diplomacy today deals with the full range of international issues: war and peace, human rights, trade, the environment, etc.  Week 6: International issues: Trade and diplomacyThis session will discuss different forms of trade disputes in international politics and how conflict can be peacefully settled. These include the operating conditions of diplomacy and the WTO’s dispute settlement mechanism in our global world.  Week 7: International issues: War and diplomacyThis session discusses what war is, and how it affects societies and politics in international relations. This session also highlights the importance of diplomacy in modern states, armed forces and wars.   Week 8: International issues: Environment and international relationsThis session will examine environmental issues in international relations and politics since 1945. We will also discuss the problems and challenges faced by global governance in solving environmental problems from different perspectives. Week 9: Human rights, individuals and cultural diplomacy in international relationsThis session will focus on human rights, individuals and people to people exchange. We will also consider if there are universal human rights in our global world.  Week 10: Guest talkA guest speaker will be invited to share with our students on the current issues related to international relations and diplomacy. Week 11: Group presentations and discussionsGroup presentations on selected topics with Q&A sessions. Week 12: The future of international relations and diplomacyThis course will examine the role that artificial intelligence plays in disrupting and shaping the future of our global politics and international law.  Week 13: Conclusion & end of term essay prepThis course will end with an account of the problems and prospects of international relations and diplomacy.

title: Introduction to International Conflicts and Sanctions
description: This course aims to teach the causes and consequences of international conflicts among nations. In particular, economic sanctions are one of the most popular mechanisms that are used to respond to security challenges. The course will begin with a foundational review of international conflicts and wars. The second part will examine how sanctions are designed and managed as a foreign policy tool. This course will provide an introduction to key debates and practices of policies on international sanctions and discuss the concept and evolution of international sanctions and their role in international conflicts.
outcome: After taking this course, students are expected to critically analyze the basic forces that shape international conflicts;  be familiar with the formulation of sanction policies; and analyze different theories and arguments in the sphere of economic sanctions.
syllabus: Week 1: Introduction to international conflicts and sanctionsThis session will examine the origins of major international conflicts. In particular, what is the geopolitical view of the distribution of power among states and what are international conflicts. This session will also discuss different types of economic sanctions and their political contexts.  Week 2: Interactions, deterrence and escalation of international conflictsThis session will discuss how deterrence has emerged as the primary resource relied on by the superpowers during the Cold War. This session will also examine how deterrence was developed and employed primarily to prevent escalation with some successful and failed cases.  Week 3: Why are sanctions imposed in international conflictsThis session will focus on who the key actors are and why sanctions are imposed in terms of the policy objectives pursued. This session will also examine the course, organization and expectations of sanctions and how the impact of sanctions can be evaluated. Week 4: The UN approach to sanctionsThis session will analyse the use of targeted sanctions by the UN Security Council (UNSC) and the transformation of the use of sanctions by the UN. Some international cases will be discussed.  Week 5: The US approach to sanctionsThis session will discuss how the US today deals with the full range of sanctions and why the US uses sanctions much more frequently than other countries since the Second World War.  Week 6: China and Russia's use of sanctionsThis session will discuss how China and Russia (the former Soviet Union) deal with sanctions. Some major cases will be evaluated.  Week 7: The EU approach to sanctionsThis session will provide an overview of EU sanctions, why they are imposed, what they do and who must comply. This session will also focus on the legal framework governing sanctions, guidance provided by the European Commission and the role of EU Member States in implementing and enforcing sanctions.  Week 8: Case study: International sanctions against IranThis session will focus on the international sanctions against Iran and the scope and impact of sanctions on society, economy and politics in Iran.  Week 9: Case study: Case study: International sanctions against RussiaThis session will focus on the international sanctions against Russia and the scope and impact of sanctions on society, economy and politics in Russia. Week 10: Alternatives of sanctions in solving international conflictsThis session will examine the impact of sanctions on our global political economy and discuss any alternatives to economic sanctions in solving international conflicts.  Week 11: Group presentations and discussionsGroup presentations on selected topics with Q&A sessions. Week 12: The future of sanctions and international conflictsThis course will examine the role of sanctions in international conflicts and how international sanctions will shape the future of our global political economy. Week 13: Conclusion & end of term essay prepThis course will end with an account of the problems and prospects of international conflicts and sanctions.

title: Political Psychology for Diplomacy and International Relations
description: This is a course focusing on those areas of political psychology most relevant to diplomacy and international relations. As such, we will start with an introduction to political psychology as its own interdisciplinary field: the study of psychological phenomena in politics or politically relevant features of psychology. Then we will cover key foundations of the relevant psychology, like social psychological biases, System 1 and 2 thought, and motivated cognition. Next we’ll explore important areas of political psychology, from system justification to moral reasoning. Then, we’ll delve into some applications of political psychology to international relations, and conclude with a bit of economic psychology of broad relevance. By the end, you should have a general grasp of political psychology as a field, and be able to incorporate psychological knowledge into your understanding of international relations and diplomacy.

title: Summer Course
description: This course is tailored for students majoring in Diplomacy and International Studies. It aims to offer a deep dive into China’s changing international relationships and the significant domestic and global factors shaping its policy making. Students will travel to a different city to analyse China’s foreign affairs in today’s international system. Prior to the trip, students will participate in preparatory seminars to gain essential background knowledge of international and China’s political economy, geopolitics, and development issues, as well as to learn basic field research methods. Through on-site visits and guided interactions, students will apply theoretical frameworks to real-world contexts and develop practical skills in diplomacy and international studies. After the fieldwork visits, students will design and undertake a research project that connects their field observations with academic analysis.

title: Navigating Conflict: Mediation and Dispute Resolution in Social Contexts
description: This 13-week undergraduate course offers a comprehensive introduction to the principles, theories, and practices of mediation and dispute resolution within a social science framework. Drawing on insights from sociology, psychology, conflict studies, and cultural anthropology, the course examines how disputes emerge in a wide range of settings—including interpersonal, community, and institutional environments.A central focus is placed on culturally sensitive approaches to mediation, with specific relevance to Hong Kong and the broader Asian context. Students are encouraged to critically engage with both local and international perspectives on conflict resolution, developing an awareness of how social and cultural factors influence dispute dynamics and outcomes.Through a blend of experiential learning—such as role-playing simulations, case analyses, and reflective exercises—students will gain practical skills that prepare them for successful careers in social work, community organization, human resources, or advanced studies in conflict resolution. Importantly, this course directly aligns with the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly Goal 16: Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions. By fostering expertise in peaceful dispute resolution and promoting inclusive, participatory methods of conflict management, the course equips students to contribute meaningfully to just and sustainable societies.

title: Field Studies
description: This course is designed to help students apply classroom learning to real-world situations in relation to diplomacy and international studies. Students will broaden their horizons and enrich their knowledge by exposure to different countries/regions. This course provides students with both individual and group learning opportunities. Students are required to participate in all activities throughout the course. These activities include but are not limited to lectures, field visits, presentations and an individual report. The destination of the course will be confirmed by the teacher who offers the course in that particular year.

title: Human Rights and Global Security in International Relations
description: This module offers an in-depth comparative analysis of the relationship between human rights and global security within the framework of international relations. By adopting a legal perspective, this course will engage with key jurisprudential theories, legal frameworks, statutory provisions and practical legal enforcement experience that underpin major geopolitical entities, including China (both Chinese mainland and Hong Kong), the United States, the United Kingdom, the European Union, and Middle Eastern countries.In particular, this course will explore the evolution and interpretation of national security laws and human rights protections across different legal systems, address the impact of major national security events on domestic and international legal norms, examine the reciprocal influence between changes of national security legislations and developments in international relations, and understand the role of domestic institutions (including the executive government, the legislature and the judiciary) and international organisations in mediating the balance between national security and human rights.By the end of the course, students will develop a nuanced understanding of how legal responses to national security challenges can both drive and reflect broader transformations in global governance and international relations.

title: Internship
description: This aim of this course is to provide students with opportunities to observe the management operations in the business, public sector or non-government organizations (NGOs) in Hong Kong or beyond, and to experience the work life in the sector, as well as to nurture students’ global vision.It is recommended that the internship to be conducted from June to August after finishing year three studies in the block mode (i.e. 5 days x 8 hours x 6 weeks). However, in case of special circumstances, students may also choose the ‘distributed mode’ (i.e. several hours in a week over a number of weeks equalling 240 hours). DIPL Programme will deploy work units, agencies, or organizations that provide internships relevant to the general course objectives. Meanwhile, students are encouraged to explore opportunities of internship to fit their own specific learning needs. However, all self-selected internship must comply with the course requirements (including the duration and nature of the internship), and subjected to the approval of DIPL Programme Director. Guidance and assistance will be provided whenever appropriate.During the internship, each student would be guided and assisted by an academic supervisor. The supervisor offers advice and help whenever necessary during the attachment period. At the same time, each student will be receiving guidance and assistance from his/her agency supervisor. Students will construct and submit a portfolio to reflect on the experience in the internship. Academic advice will be provided to help students consolidate their learning in the internship.

title: Capstone Project
description: The aim of this course is to provide students with learning opportunities to undertake a final Capstone Project before graduation. Students are required to form groups and design a project on selected topics related to current global affairs or diplomatic issues under the supervision of a faculty member. Students need to integrate and apply knowledge and techniques from their courses, overseas exchange, and internships to develop and complete a real-world analytical and diplomatic project. Students are encouraged to think out of the box and can submit their projects in any format such as a development project, video, website as agreed upon with their supervisor.
